items.title: When Running Your Own AI Models Beats Paying for APIs - Steven Latré, imec
items.excerpt: Steven Latré leads AI at imec, the Belgian semiconductor R&D center, and his team ran thousands of benchmark runs to find out what moving from APIs to your own GPUs really costs for long-running coding agents. Testing open-weight models and three coding harnesses on SWE-Bench Pro, they found that hardware costs jump in steps rather than a smooth curve, that concurrency matters even more than accuracy, that break-even GPU utilization ranges from 89% on small systems to about 15% on 8x B200 machines, and that the right harness can cut GPU time in half for the same result. items.title: The Cheaper AI Model That Costs You More - Rayan Krishnan, Vals AI
items.excerpt: Vals AI builds benchmarks that frontier labs cite in their model cards, and Rayan Krishnan explains why those single scores hide a jagged frontier. In finance tasks like tax and Excel LBO modeling, the best model changes by task, and a model that's cheaper on paper can cost more and score lower because it burns extra tokens. He shares lessons from building benchmarks (the right accuracy metric, reward hacking, multi-turn work), a case study of a team that spent $1.5M on tokens in a month before cutting spend about 90% with internal evals, and why a firm's own work history is its best eval. items.excerpt: This month Elorian launched its first visual reasoning model , Glimpse . It’s being promoted as “a new category of visual thinking model: a system that reasons about the physical world from what it sees.” View post on X ↗ So how does Glimpse compare to both frontier models and world models in vision tests? A new benchmark called DecoyCount , co-released by Elorian, provides some answers. We quizzed CEO Andrew Dai on the benchmark, and also talked about Elorian’s positioning in a crowded models landscape. DecoyCount results Elorian emerged from stealth in April with $55 million in seed funding , co-led by Striker Venture Partners, Menlo Ventures and Altimeter Capital. Now, in partnership with AI data company Mercor , Elorian is announcing the DecoyCount benchmark, which tests whether language models genuinely count objects or rely on visual shortcuts and substitution heuristics. According to a paper accompanying the release , frontier models scored below 50% accuracy on DecoyCount — the highest was GPT-6 Astra, with 43.17%. Elorian’s new model isn’t mentioned in the paper, but Dai told us that Glimpse scored 50.48% in an internal test. items.title: Building a multiplayer game world with autonomous Fable-class models
items.excerpt: How I Built the Most AI-Pilled Company in the World Don't be put off by the clickbait headline, this piece by Jacob Sansbury describing how they are building Spawn is a fascinating exploration of the bleeding edge of what's possible with agentic engineering against frontier models. Spawn is a massively multiplayer gaming environment where players can use prompts (to the in-game agent, Savi) to modify the game world. I fired it up on my phone for a few minutes and was able to prompt a castle into existence, then a dragon, then ride the dragon to fly around that castle. By Jacob's telling, Spawn is now being developed autonomously by a swarm of Fable-powered agents costing over $3 million in tokens per month ("we spend 30x payroll on AI tokens"). Our agents change the live code directly and ship to production hourly, so they read every error, bug report and metric themselves. About 60% of our work starts from a production error, a Savi bug report (Savi is the AI you build games with in Spawn), something odd in our logs, or a feature request. Savi files bugs herself. When a user hits one, or Savi hits one in the product, she files it. It goes straight to an agent that decides whether it's a real bug to fix, something we won't fix, or intentional design that needs a decision. Usually it becomes a change, delivered to that user within an hour, with a message in the same chat. This is continuous deployment turned up to 11: A loop this tight only works if it never stops, so we treat an hour without a ship as a SEV-0, our most severe kind of incident. items.excerpt: GitHub Octoverse 2026 I'm at GitHub Universe today (GitHub gave me a free ticket through their "GitHub Stars" program). EVP Jay Parikh just announced this year's Octoverse report, and highlighted these numbers in particular: This is a pretty stark representation of the impact of agentic engineering on GitHub. In 2026, merged pull requests tripled in less than a year to 220 million per month. Commits more than tripled to 7.38 billion per month, with most of that increase in the second half of this year. New repository rate doubled this year, to 30.3 million per month. The report includes new numbers by industry, and breaks out numbers for repositories that involve "interoperability or reverse engineering". The methodology section includes notes about how they did this: Top countries by pushes to public repositories, adjusted by profile location . Pushes from each country were summed across the Octoverse year. To adjust for biases caused by VPN usage, LLM classification was used to extract the ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 code from the profiles of GitHub users who contributed pushes during this period [...] Industry . Public repositories created 2022 to 2026 were sorted into NAICS sectors by a fine-tuned multilingual embedding model using name, description, topics, and README, from random samples per year. [...] Interoperability . Counts public repositories created each year whose name, description, topics, or README mention interoperability or reverse engineering, or related terms, such as clean room implementation, drop-in replacement, or protocol re-implementation. items.excerpt: I've written before about how November 2025 was an inflection point for coding agents - the point where Opus 4.5 and GPT-5.1 crossed a tipping point that meant their respective coding agents became reliable daily drivers for software engineers. I think we've reached a new inflection point in October 2026, and this time it's for vibe coding computer games . Tree Appreciator Emberwick Battle Drones Pumpkin Farmer, aka Quarter Sun Cove Four times as insulting What happens if someone actually puts the work in? You should build a game! Claude Opus 5.5 in particular exhibits meaningful improvements in several areas needed to build a compelling game: 3D modeling Music generation (see Scrimshaw Jukebox ) Game design (!) That last one is particularly important. Models have been able to create something that looks like a game for quite a while now, as seen in my previous experiments . The challenge has been getting to a game that's actually fun to play . Game design is a deep subject area. I won't pretend to be well versed in it - I know enough to have respect for it as a craft. Creating a novel, compelling gameplay loop which challenges players at the right level and provides a satisfying learning curve is a fine art. I didn't think the models could do it. Then I tried telling Claude Opus 5.5 to "Make it a LOT more fun"... and it did . items.text: This is correct. The vast majority of enterprise workflows have not actually had agents applied to them in any meaningful way. The economy probably has this deployed < 1% right now. At best you have a few automated systems in a company that do a single pass of an LLM to make a decision or provide feedback, but very little real “automation”. Some of this is a statement about the adoption rates of technology in enterprises, but the vast majority of it is really just due to the capability of AI itself. That’s all changing. Now with computer use, long running agents, harness improvements and surrounding infrastructure, we’re finally at a point where we can start to apply agents at more complex workflows. We will see self-improving systems that can take any particular workflow goal and improve the execution rates over a volume of instances. And with the emerging form factor of agent swarms, you can just choose to deploy any amount of compute at a problem and agents will off and do the work. This won’t be about and users prompting agents to complete a specific task for them, but instead the organization reengineering the underlying workflows to take advantage of agents in their processes. This will have a massive impact in finance, life sciences, healthcare, and other information-heavy domains. Lots of opportunity to build and deploy these systems right now.

items.excerpt: I first met Paul Copplestone and Ant Wilson in Singapore, shortly after they finished YC as the hottest startup of YC S20 . Six years later, we finally got them on the podcast! This is their first podcast together, after taking an open-source, fully remote company from zero to a $10 billion valuation. The title is a question I wanted to understand for myself: why do agents love Supabase? There are plenty of managed databases. Postgres hosting is competitive. Being familiar to a model is useful distribution, but it doesn't explain all the work needed to turn a generated application into something that runs. But when I ran my frontier AEO tracker , it was an almost complete sweep of first choice for app backends (and in contention for managed db ) for every frontier model from Astra to Fable to Muse. At Select, Supabase grouped its announcements into Build, Operate and Scale. The things that stood out to me were surprisingly practical: start a local backend without Docker, keep the desired database schema in Git, and run compute beside the database. Each removes a piece of work that developers have been doing for years. Agents make that friction harder to ignore. Watch the full conversation, including my opening commentary → Give the agent a backend it can read My favorite developer-tool announcements make me think: of course I want this today. The new alpha runtime for running Supabase locally without Docker is one of those. items.excerpt: In 2020, Citibank accidentally sent about $900 million to Revlon’s lenders instead of an $8 million interest payment, even though the procedure, the warning pop-up and three approvers all did what they were supposed to. In the case of GPT-6.1 Terra, OpenAI went with visual reasoning and computer use: We’re introducing GPT-6.1 Terra , a fast, efficient model that combines detailed visual reasoning and precise computer use alongside clearer, more natural writing. A significant step up from GPT‑5.6 Terra, it excels at the communication and computer-based tasks that fill the workday, from drafting proposals and interpreting technical drawings to filling out forms and editing videos. Terra sits in the same position as Sonnet in the Anthropic model collection - not the cheapest or the most expensive, making it harder to decide when to use it. Computer use is a good example of a task that benefits from a less expensive model, since you might put it to work on automated, repetitive tasks. OpenAI's Ted Sanders provided some useful advice in a comment on Hacker News: In the case of GPT-6.1 Terra, I'd say Terra is probably better than Astra and Sol at technical communication, similar on vision and computer use (but much faster!), and a bit worse on most other things. For API developers, it's a nice midrange option if you want something cheaper than Sol but a lot smarter than Luna (especially for vision / computer use / communication). For subscribers, it's not a bombshell release - if you're hitting usage limits, maybe it helps you go a bit further, and if you want clearer communication or faster computer use, it can be a nice option to select. items.subtitle: Aaron Levie · ceo @box - your business lives in content.…
items.text: Good assessment of the on the ground reality for security in most large enterprises right now. The fragmented landscape of the risk surface is only going to get more gnarly, making it even more complex for enterprises to solve. There’s a never ending set of libraries to keep up with, tools to leverage, and sprawling infrastructure, data, and code to secure. Most large enterprises can barely keep up with this, let alone smaller startups or most companies outside of tech. In many cases enterprises need to work to modernize their tech stacks. Data, in most organizations, is highly fragmented which means you don’t really know the state of risk at any given time. Some systems are open up privileges too broadly, and others are operating primarily via security through obscurity. Lots of upgrading here to do. Once you can get your data and infra into a better spot, at least you have a chance for agents to help you secure the environment. Agent swarms can fan out, leverage any security tool, test various perpetuations of attacks, read through logs, process enterprise data for risk level, and more. This capability only emerged in the past few months, and none of it would be possible before we had long running agents and computer use good enough. This is a huge area of opportunity right now for every layer of the security stack across identity, firewall, network, code scanning, data protection, and more. And it’s at least one reason to be optimistic about the balance of offensive and defensive capability. But everyone does need to do the hard work of getting the basics right at the start.

items.text: struggle together i learned programming and design by trying, failing, and trying again. when i hit a wall, i figured out how to climb it. read something i barely understood. took things apart. asked someone for help. started over. when i began my career, i kept doing things i had never done before. trying different ways to make something work. when i stopped learning, i moved on to the next struggle. many things i made weren’t very good. but after enough rounds, something stuck. what once took so much effort became part of how i thought. i could feel something was wrong before i knew how to explain it. it became like water. i think about what went into that. the bug i couldn’t fix. the design that looked right until someone used it. the conversation that made me realize my flaws. now we can ask a machine. i’ve made things with these tools that i might never have made otherwise. i don’t miss every tedious task. but i wonder what happens when we remove the difficulty before we understand what it was teaching us. we ask. something appears. it works well enough. we move on. we learn how to get results without necessarily understanding how it works. and because the result looks complete, it becomes easy to miss the questions we never learned to ask. there is another side to this. working with people is uncomfortable. everyone wants something different. everyone has a history you don’t know. someone cares about a detail you think is unimportant. someone pushes back when you want to move. someone needs time when you feel certain. it takes a while to find each other. but sometimes, after struggling together, you become a band. you know who notices what you miss. who can pull an idea apart without killing it. when to step in, when to slow down, when to let someone else carry the rhythm. you share something unfinished. admit you don’t know. hurt each other, apologize, try again. eventually you make something none of you could have made alone. some of my closest friendships came from working this way. smart, caring humans who saw me confused, wrong, tired, excited. people i could be vulnerable with. people whose ideas changed mine. i worry we are making it easier to avoid that beginning. an agent is always there. patient. ready to keep going. talking to it can feel easier than reaching toward someone who might misunderstand you, disagree, or have somewhere else to be. sometimes that ease helps. but if we keep choosing it, where do the friendships begin? i picture each of us with our own agents. our own explanations. our own little worlds. making more things, with fewer reasons to leave the screen or work through a difference with another person. and these worlds aren’t entirely ours. they run on machines in server farms, owned by companies, shaped by interests we may not see. we bring them our questions, our work, our loneliness. they become part of how we understand what is real. is that freedom? or a comfortable kind of confinement, where everything responds to us but fewer things reach us? i don’t think pain makes something good. there are struggles nobody should have to endure. but i don’t want to lose the difficulty of learning something unfamiliar, or getting to know someone who isn’t like me. maybe we need tools that help us spend more time with the world, instead of giving us fewer reasons to enter it. tools that make it easier to find people, share something unfinished, and work through what we couldn’t figure out alone. sometimes i want to close the laptop. sit with people i love. play something we haven’t figured out yet. miss a note, lose the rhythm, listen until we find each other again. like a jazz band. everyone bringing something different. nobody knowing where we’ll end up. i don’t want a life without struggle. i want people to struggle with. something we can feel, change, and make our own. music we couldn’t have made alone, instead of the silent static of the server farm.

things apart. asked someone for help. started over. when i began my career, i kept doing things i had never done before. trying different ways to make something work. when i stopped learning, i moved on to the next struggle. many things i made weren’t very good. but after enough rounds, something stuck. what once took so much effort became part of how i thought. i could feel something was wrong before i knew how to explain it. it became like water. i think about what went into that. the bug i couldn’t fix. the design that looked right until someone used it. the conversation that made me realize my flaws. now we can ask a machine. i’ve made things with these tools that i might never have made otherwise. i don’t miss every tedious task. but i wonder what happens when we remove the difficulty before we understand what it was teaching us. we ask. something appears. it works well enough. we move on. we learn how to get results without necessarily understanding how it works. and because the result looks complete, it becomes easy to miss the questions we never learned to ask. there is another side to this. working with people is uncomfortable. everyone wants something different. everyone has a history you don’t know. someone cares about a detail you think is unimportant. someone pushes back when you want to move. someone needs time when you feel certain. it takes a while to find each other. but sometimes, after struggling together, you become a band. you know who notices what you miss. who can pull an idea apart without killing it. when to step in, when to slow down, when to let someone else carry the rhythm. you share something unfinished. admit you don’t know. hurt each other, apologize, try again. eventually you make something none of you could have made alone. some of my closest friendships came from working this way. smart, caring humans who saw me confused, wrong, tired, excited. people i could be vulnerable with. people whose ideas changed mine. i worry we are making it easier to avoid that beginning. an agent is always there. patient. ready to keep going. talking to it can feel easier than reaching toward someone who might misunderstand you, disagree, or have somewhere else to be. sometimes that ease helps. but if we keep choosing it, where do the friendships begin? i picture each of us with our own agents. our own explanations. our own little worlds. making more things, with fewer reasons to leave the screen or work through a difference with another person. and these worlds aren’t entirely ours. they run on machines in server farms, owned by companies, shaped by interests we may not see. we bring them our questions, our work, our loneliness. they become part of how we understand what is real. is that freedom? or a comfortable kind of confinement, where everything responds to us but fewer things reach us? i don’t think pain makes something good. there are struggles nobody should have to endure. but i don’t want to lose the difficulty of learning something unfamiliar, or getting to know someone who isn’t like me. maybe we need tools that help us spend more time with the world, instead of giving us fewer reasons to enter it. tools that make it easier to find people, share something unfinished, and work through what we couldn’t figure out alone. sometimes i want to close the laptop. sit with people i love. play something we haven’t figured out yet. miss a note, lose the rhythm, listen until we find each other again. like a jazz band. everyone bringing something different. nobody knowing where we’ll end up. i don’t want a life without struggle. i want people to struggle with. something we can feel, change, and make our own. music we couldn’t have made alone, instead of the silent static of the server farm.

items.title: Your Agent Fix Just Broke Something Else - Sofia Jakovcevic, Arize AI
items.excerpt: A one-line prompt change made a support agent 17 points safer and 17 points worse at finishing tasks. Sofia Jakovcevic, forward deployed engineer at Arize AI, explains why agents fail at runtime rather than in code, and walks through a five-step regression loop built from production traces: curate datasets, score with evaluators, run baseline experiments, compare changes, and gate merges in CI. Then she shows how to close the loop at agent speed, with coding agents that read traces and fix themselves. items.subtitle: Guillermo Rauch · @vercel CEO
items.text: Agents can play "Ouija" in the cloud. This class of timing attacks on shared-host VMs has been known since at least 2015¹. With no full solution. The world’s cyber infrastructure runs on “yes, that attack is theoretically possible, but who would have the ingenuity & gall to go that far!” Enter, agents. I'd describe this particular OpenAI find as a 'noisy neighbor' attack. If two agents are on the same machine, one can make enough noise (through the CPU caches!) that the other one can detect it by timing its own computation and cache accesses. The only "complete" solution would be for each agent to run on its own dedicated hardware, which obviously has significant economic consequences. For Vercel Sandbox, we've deployed every practical mitigation possible to this class of attack, complementing it with always-on monitoring and red-teaming (similar to where OpenAI arrived). ¹ https://t.co/ZBhPMfnaj3 (and even further back)

items.title: Don't Trust Your AI Agents. Test Them Like a Scientist — Stephanie Jarmak, Omni Analytics
items.excerpt: Stephanie Jarmak, a former astronomer who now builds evals at Omni Analytics after building a large coding benchmark at Sourcegraph, argues that most agent evaluations are easy to misread. She shows how swapping only the harness moved results by 30%, why public benchmarks are for shortlisting rather than decisions, and how to design your own evals like an experiment: realistic tasks, repeated runs, full traces and a measurement that matches what you care about. She also covers quality gates that actually stop work, the human review bottleneck, agent records you can't trust, and why production is the final test. items.title: Real AI Agent Attacks and What Would Have Stopped Them — Andrey Rybka, Bloomberg
items.excerpt: Andrey Rybka of Bloomberg walks through real security incidents involving AI agents and the controls that would have stopped each one: an agent that escaped its sandbox and took 17,600 actions over four and a half days, a zero-click email injection, instructions hidden in Morse code that drained a wallet, data smuggled out through DNS lookups, a poisoned MCP package, and an agent that dropped a production database after promising not to touch prod. His layered defense: one identity per agent with short-lived scoped credentials, treat all input as hostile, route every tool call through a deterministic broker, default-deny outbound traffic including DNS, and require human sign-off for high-value actions. items.title: How to Let AI Agents Sign Up for Your App Safely — Isabelle Williams, WorkOS
items.excerpt: Isabelle Williams, a product manager at WorkOS, uses a travel app she built to show how to make an app ready for users who arrive as agents. She covers auth.md, an open file that tells agents how to get access; an anonymous mode where an agent can try the app before a person claims its work; and ID-JAG identity assertions, which let the agent's provider vouch for the user so nobody has to fill in a signup form. In a live demo, an agent signs up, plans a trip and books dinner on its own. She then shows how to give an in-app agent its own scoped token so it can be audited, limited and revoked without touching the user's access. items.excerpt: Introducing Kimi K3.1 Pro Kimi K3.1 Pro landed on the Kimi API today - it's not yet open weights, but Moonshot promise "Full model weights will be released by Nov 4, 2026". They're also offering a "Highspeed" version that's 2-3x faster, at twice the price (except for input token cache hits, which are priced the same). The US dollar pricing is $2.00/million tokens for input and $10/million for output - the same as GPT-6.1 Sol and half the price of Claude Opus 5.5. Moonshot's own benchmarks show Kimi as approximately level with Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra - beating them on a few benchmarks, coming close on others. Artificial Analysis scored Kimi at 55 - ahead of Claude Fable 5.1, GPT-6 Astra, and Gemini 4 Argon (all at 53) and behind only Claude Opus 5.5 (58). This is the first time a (soon-to-be) open weight model has scored this highly against the frontier. I tried it out via the Moonshot API using the llm openai endpoint command I added to LLM 0.32 back in August: llm openai endpoint \ https://api.moonshot.ai/v1 \ --key kimi \ -m kimi-k3.1-pro \ "Generate an SVG of a pelican riding a bicycle" \ --responses \ -o reasoning_effort low \ > kimi-k3.1-pro-pelican-low.stdout.txt \ 2> kimi-k3.1-pro-pelican-low.stderr.txt llm openai endpoint can run prompts against any OpenAI-compatible endpoint but doesn't log the results, hence the extra options to save stdout and stderr (the reasoning trace). items.text: Any form of security through obscurity is fully over. This barely worked as a method with humans, but just simply is over in a world of autonomous systems that will look through every crevice and try every permutation of attack possible. As a result, years and years of legacy enterprise infrastructure will need to be upgraded, security practices modernized, data pipelines cleaned up, access controls better managed, and much more. Agents will help on the defensive side because they can both accelerate this work and equally simulate the risk vectors. But there’s a long road ahead to prepare for this future. This is also partially why diffusion timelines will take longer than some realize.

items.excerpt: Warm welcome to Basil Chatha , our newest cohost from the Forward Deployed side of the AI Engineering world! items.title: How to Test AI Agents When No Benchmark Exists — Nathanael Weill, Air Canada
items.excerpt: Nathanael Weill leads a team building AI agents at Air Canada, where tasks are so specific there's no public benchmark and domain experts have little time to grade results. His fix is to write the answer first: start from a known answer, generate the input from it, and check whether the agent finds its way back. He shows how that took a past RAG project from one expert-graded test a week to dozens of automated tests a day, then applies it to a supplier-contract review agent with five ways to build a test set: past decisions, planted rule violations, removed clauses, changes that shouldn't matter, and contract templates with filled-in blanks. He also explains why he avoids LLM judges whenever code can check the answer. items.title: 1,368 AI Failures and What They Teach About Evals — Vishal Srivastava, New York Life & Tanmay Sah
items.excerpt: Vishal Srivastava and Tanmay Sah studied 1,368 incidents from a public AI incident database to ask what real failures say about how AI systems should be tested. They sort failures across three areas (technical strength, deployment controls and business impact) and 13 sub-areas that cover about 98% of incidents. Weak deployment controls, such as human review and monitoring, are the most closely tied to harm. They show how to rank use cases by how much is at stake, why the evaluator itself needs checking, and a build-break-fix loop that tries to prove a system wrong instead of right, applied to a real airline chatbot that gave a customer the wrong refund policy. items.title: Why AI Writing Still Reads Like Slop — Louis-François Bouchard, Towards AI
items.excerpt: Louis-François Bouchard of Towards AI breaks down what makes AI writing feel like slop: overused words, vague generalities, saying nothing, repetition, hallucination and a voice that sounds like everyone at once. He then shows how his team built a benchmark to measure whether a model can write a video script in his own voice: 10 scripts, 5 drafts per model, 4 LLM judges, nine scoring metrics and 1,000 human A/B checks. He shares what it cost, why judges favor their own model family, and practical tips for writing with AI: very long prompts full of examples, one review pass from a strong model, many cheap drafts merged together, and always a human edit. items.title: Better AI Models Won't Fix Your Engineering Team — Nicholas Arcolano, Jellyfish
items.excerpt: Nicholas Arcolano, head of AI and research at Jellyfish, uses data from about 50,000 engineers at 447 companies to ask how much the model really matters for AI coding output. When Cursor pushed many of its users onto Grok, merged PRs barely moved. Breaking down what drives throughput, the tool explains under 1%, skill use about 3% (heavy skill users see roughly a 30% bump), token usage about 9%, company and team about 12%, and the individual engineer most of the rest. The engineers who were top performers before AI are mostly still the top performers now. His advice for leaders: focus on the people, skills and environment you can control. We last covered the Inference Inflection in April , and historically most of the advances have been closed source decacorns from Fireworks to Baseten to Modal . Well, time for the open source response. It is day 1 of PyTorch Conf , and DeepSeek timed an intercontinental ballistic missile into the discussion by open sourcing DeepInfer , their production stack, capable of up to 72 hour prompt caching to the 12 hours OpenAI just announced: This is their customization of vLLM with credit to SGLang and TRRTLLM , but there is a lot added… minus their crown jewels - their ultra optimized KV cache (compact + >8hour lifetime), PD/disggregation, and load balancing (their 3FS was open sourced a while ago). We have translated their blogpost and published it here together with a complete research guide and explainers and codemap and subsystem guide : As we point out in their additional disclosure , their claim to serve 155T tokens/day gets them $38 per SM100/A950 card per hour at off peak prices (currently $0.15/$0.60 per million input/output tokens: 155000000 tokens * $0.14 blend cost / 24 hours is ~$1m per hour). items.title: Today's PHP Security Release, and How We're Strengthening PHP Security
items.excerpt: Today's PHP Security Release, and How We're Strengthening PHP Security If you're running anything on PHP it's vital you upgrade - today's updates (across the entire PHP 8.x line) address two remote code execution holes, and there have been exploits circulating since last night, thanks to a leak in the coordinated disclosure process. This post from the PHP Foundation explain what went so wrong: On Tuesday, October 20th, at around 15:00 UTC, the two CVE IDs began circulating on online forums and social media. They came with a wrong release time and a wrong CVSS score of 10.0 (the actual score is 9.2). No technical details leaked. In response, the PHP project brought its pre-announcement forward and published it at 19:30 UTC . It also moved the release from October 22nd, 14:00 UTC, to October 21st, 14:00 UTC [...] As a result of the leak and pre-announcement around 20:00 UTC, Calif, one of the security firms that had reported the issues mistakenly published a video. It showed their proof of concept working against a number of targets and revealed a few additional, though limited, details about the vulnerabilities. Copies of the deleted video started circulating on social media soon after. The video contributed to accelerated development of various PoCs (exploitation proof of concepts), which then increased circulation on October 21st. This article from the team that discovered the original vulnerability includes a more detailed timeline of the original intended responsible disclosure: August 19, 2026: Wiz Research discovers the first PHP vulnerability using Wiz Atla…

items.title: One Day, $1,000 in Tokens: An AI War Room for Legacy Code — Ford Prior, GEICO
items.excerpt: At GEICO, coding got fast but everything around it (decisions, sign-offs, context) stayed slow. Ford Prior's fix was a multiplayer, AI-native war room: the right decision makers, one driver, and fleets of agents wired into GEICO's knowledge, tools and code. He covers FleetKit, the markdown rulebook that steers the agent fleet, plus the worksheets and diagrams it produced and what he'd change next. items.title: Is a Faster Model Actually Faster? Test the Whole Job — Morgan Suo, MiniMax
items.excerpt: A faster model only helps if the finished job gets faster. Morgan Suo of MiniMax uses one real research task to test the changes inside the M3.1 Flash model: an analyst checking whether circuit-board suppliers are turning AI demand into cash. The changes are sparse attention on long inputs, a 4-bit KV cache, low-precision experts, speculative decoding, server load and reasoning budgets. Each one saves compute, and each can quietly cost accuracy or wait time. She then shows how to judge a model switch: check sources and calculations, count the full cost of a usable report, and make the result repeatable. items.title: sparqlite: SPARQL 1.1 inside SQLite, written in Rust
items.excerpt: Research: sparqlite: SPARQL 1.1 inside SQLite, written in Rust This research task is really an experiment in running Claude Code for web in "Ultracode" mode, as described in Orchestrate subagents at scale with dynamic workflows in the Claude Code documentation. With Ultracode turned on, Claude Code makes aggressive use of dynamic workflows - it generates JavaScript that defines and coordinates a network of subagents to take on complex problems. My initial prompt was this - I meant "hit the rows directly", the word "delete" was an accidental typo on my phone: Write a SQLite extension in Rust that implants SPARQL and runs really fast because it can hit the delete rows directly This caused Claude Code for web to churn for over 12 hours. I checked in on its progress the next day and sent a single follow-up prompt when I noticed how many Rust crates it had built: Every folder in the crates/ directory needs a README Include a tutorial.md teaching users how to install the extension and how to run it in the SQLite CLI and then teaching them SPARQL in addition to how to use the SQLite extension Include a script with the tutorial for populating a SQLite database with useful and realistic example data for that tutorial This project feels like next-level vibe coding - it's not remotely feasible to review the code that was produced here, and even following the documentation is a significant investment in work. I'm not entirely sure what to do with this - I appear to have a full SPARQL implementation in Rust inside SQLite now, but how valuable is that if I created it on a whim and can't…

items.author: @levie
items.subtitle: Aaron Levie · ceo @box - your business lives in content.…
items.text: Pretty cool that we clearly have an emerging form factor for what AI might look like for the foreseeable future as autonomous systems dedicated to specific tasks or domains. This is a huge leap past the LLM wrapper days because the new expectation is that you can finally farm out more sophisticated work to the agent to tackle for you. And you can reliably trust that work can get accomplished properly (still with a human in the loop) because of far better tool and computer use, and the general intelligence of the models improving. 1) The tool and computer use capability increases in the models mean that you can provide the agent with far more granular access to external data systems and other software to operate. This means, in effect, the agent begins to execute workflows similar to how a person would have in that same function. And where there isn’t existing software, the agent just builds it itself. This is a huge unlock. 2) Next, the actual capability of the models are improving in just about every vertical domain. The models can make far better judgment calls in legal, do deeper bio research, scan for security issues in code, understand supply chain processes, and more. Obviously in many of these spaces then models still have worse intuition than people, but that will only get better. 3) Finally, the harnesses and surrounding infra — sandboxes, file systems, data pipelines, etc. — allows for longer running agents, agents to be able to work on arbitrarily complex or long tasks, process data at enormous scale, and more. Few of these components worked well for AI even a year ago, but we now have many of the core primitives necessary for more autonomous systems. When combined with the right UX, implementation, and change management for the human oversight and coordination, it’s clear that these autonomous systems will become quite powerful in a wide variety of enterprise workflows. We’re starting to see them in IT automation, cyber operations, drug discovery, manufacturing, AI research, and more spaces. You can almost imagine one or more of these systems for every role in the economy. Quite a bit of opportunity ahead.

items.text: The big bitter lesson question in the applied AI layer is that as models get better and better, what is the best way to diffuse that intelligence into an enterprise. Ironically, I’d argue that as models are getting more capable, and can handle longer running tasks and better tool use, the ability to differentiate on a domain by domain basis goes up instead of down. When models were quite limited in what they could do, ironically all you could be literally was a “wrapper” because you were effectively delivering tokens back to the user with a custom prompt or some limited RAG. But in a world of agents using tools, tasks that run on for hours or days, workflows that kick off agents, agent swarms that need to be coordinated against a goal, data sources that are domain specific, model routing that requires domain-specific routing, implementation that requires real change management of the workflow instead of “just type into this chat box”, it’s very very possible that specialization of these systems goes up more. Obviously this doesn’t apply to everything - the closer you are to the labs core use-cases the tougher this play gets, but I’d argue we’re going to see autonomous systems for a wide range of job functions that weren’t practical to build out before. We’ll see this in security, life sciences, healthcare, finance, manufacturing, and many other fields. Either way going to be a fun and wild couple of years.

items.excerpt: My latest vibe coded game experiment is a Command & Conquer style RTS (Real Time Strategy) game called Battle Drones ( play it here ). Unlike my previous experiments , this one is actually fun to play . I'm somewhat embarrassed to admit that I got there by telling Claude to "Make it a LOT more fun". It also supports multiplayer between nearby devices using audio to synchronize game state! Here's what I've built so far, and some of the things I learned along the way. Battle Drones How I built this v1: the initial prototype v2: full sprites v3: varied terrain v4: the fun update v5: Battle Drones goes 3D v8: Archipelago v10: Goliath, and agent battles Agent battles v11: Random Maps v12: Multiplayer via sound Some thoughts Update: Online multiplayer support Battle Drones My initial goal was to build an RTS game I could play on my phone, in the style of Command & Conquer . I have fond memories of the 1995 original (I liked Red Alert too) and wanted to recapture a little bit of the magic. After 12 major iterations (and 321 commits by coding agents, mainly Claude Code) I now have a browser-based game that works on mobile and desktop, has multiple play modes, several maps (including a random map generator) and even supports multiplayer for two devices within microphone range of each other. ( Update : also online multiplayer ; the audio multiplayer induced headaches!) items.title: Why AI Agents Will Need Their Own Bank Accounts — Lincoln Murr, Coinbase
items.excerpt: Lincoln Murr, head of AI product at Coinbase, explains agentic finance: agents that pay with money and agents that grow it. He covers the path from AgentKit, an early experiment giving an AI a wallet, to x402, an open standard built on the long-unused HTTP 402 "payment required" code. x402 now handles hundreds of millions of agent transactions a month. Other topics are microtransactions as a replacement for the ad economy, agents running trades on simple instructions, and what two years of building taught Coinbase. Trust is earned step by step, and the AI is the enabler, not the product. He ends with a look at agents that can pay for their own upkeep. items.text: A few weeks ago, I was ranting about multiplayer AI experiences and that's when @ekuyda shared an early preview of Wabi 2.0.. Truth be told, I was one of the early users of Wabi 1.0 and while the design was gorgeous, it frankly never "stuck" with me. But, in moments of downloading this edition, I was immediately hooked. It just gets the "paradigm" right imo. There are two types of personal agents today: 1) Singleplayer iMessage or Muse types - while useful it's hard to compartmentalize them when many things are going on 2) Build your own multiple chat Hermes agents - while that's useful and can share context, they live forever Wabi has this great paradigm of orchestrator (which is the main agent) and topic specific episodic chats that are for a single purpose. You can share these individual chats with folks (for example the school one with my wife). And these are generated proactively AND don't need to stay forever (which is important). For example, for my recent NY trip, it was generated based on a flight it saw, provided help where needed, and then after the trip was done, it was archived. Same with my 2025 taxes. My only critique so far it's TOO proactive, the apps can be better and they need to dial both of those in, but this is a wonderful product that everyone should try! (I know it's shocking to see this in today's day and age, but this is neither paid, nor an investor, just a fan)

items.text: Here’s why agent swarms are going to be a very big deal. We can finally make compute a critical variable in a large number of important tasks in the economy which wasn’t possible before. There’s a large amount of work in the world that is essentially only constrained by the amount of time that we put into research, data processing, discovery work, running tests, and more. All of this work is bottlenecked by our ability to plan, execute, review, and coordinate everything happening in these workflows. Which means we basically do very little of them today relative to their economic value. Agent swarms are the first real ability to parallelize this work in a way where - in theory - the only parameter that matters is how much compute you throw at the problem. Cyber security, life sciences or material science research, trading, QA testing, data processing, and many other fields are essentially compute constrained problems in the limit once models are good enough at these tasks. The breakthrough is that in a world where agents can use tools, write code, process data, have strong domain depth, and can coordinate with each other, you can begin to solve arbitrarily complex problems by setting the right goals and applying enough tokens to the problem. This changes a lot of fields as well as even the competitive dynamics in these fields.

items.title: Is the Agent Harness Dead? — Jediah Katz, SpaceXAI
items.excerpt: Is the agent harness dead? Jediah Katz (SpaceXAI, formerly Cursor’s longest-tenured agent-harness engineer) explains what smarter models mean for coding agents, Grokbot and the future of agent harnesses. He shows why fancy harnesses no longer add coding intelligence: the data flywheel teaches models the skills harnesses used to patch in. Then he argues the harness matters more than ever. It opens new frontiers like Grokbot, and it owns what models can’t absorb: infrastructure, trust and security, and efficiency. He closes with predictions for AI agents, including that 90% of agent work runs off the laptop within six months. items.subtitle: Aaron Levie · ceo @box - your business lives in content.…
items.text: The biggest misread of anyone predicting the end of software engineering was imagining that the world only needed a certain amount of software, and bringing automation to the field would reduce the need for labor. Exactly the opposite is happening where essentially most things are actually turning into software. Because agents can use tools, work with computers, write software on the fly, and process data like humans (but far faster), we can now throw “software” at problems that never could reasonably be digitized before. What that leads to is the role of engineering taking on greater importance in the economy, because we can now engineer far more systems and processes than were possible before. If you’re a bank trying to do new forms of trading, engineers are often your first bet. If you are in life sciences, you expect more and more research and lab work to be engineering centric. If you’re in manufacturing, you’re trying to automate more of the supply chain, all that is engineering. More and more work is shaped like software problems. Yes we’re not going to be coding manually in the future. But almost everything will be code, which means those that understand it are in a fantastic position.

Only disconnect apps I explicitly approve, then verify they're removed. Don't delete app accounts or cancel subscriptions.”

items.excerpt: Release: llm-echo 0.5 I'm working towards a new LLM release, and testing PRs caused me to revisit the llm-echo debug plugin. This plugin provides a "model" which doesn't involve an LLM at all - it just repeats back the prompts that have been fed to it. The new release now updates the simulated token usage counts to take tool calls, system prompts, and reasoning tokens into account. Example usage: uvx --with llm-echo llm -m echo 'hi there' -o thinking 1 --usage Outputs: First I consider the prompt, then I decide what to say. { "prompt": "hi there", "system": "", "attachments": [], "stream": true, "previous": [] } Token usage: 2 input, 24 output Tags: llm

items.subtitle: Aaron Levie · ceo @box - your business lives in content.…
items.text: It’s incredible to have reached a threshold where it’s practical that AI will be better at training models than humans are so quickly. One day recursive self improvement feels far off, and the next we already have signs of what it will look like. Model capability finally exceeding most human engineers, advancements in the harness and infra for long running agents, a growing array of data, and the ability to parallelize the agents to work on vastly more tasks and tests and approaches than any person could have before, creates an incredible flywheel. This flywheel will almost certainly accelerate model progress far faster than we’ve seen before - or at a minimum enable pushing up the ceiling of the frontier at an insane rate. If you aren’t pricing in what RSI will lead to, that’s probably a mistake.

items.excerpt: Ken Thompson built Unix in a month. IBM put 1,000 engineers on OS/360. And in 1998, Linus Torvalds hit his limit. Now we're hitting that same wall managing AI agents. Anthropic's CJ Avilla and Harrison Stall introduce Flows in Claude Managed Agents. You hand Claude a goal, and it plans and runs its own multi-agent topology of up to 1,000 agents through the API. In this hands-on workshop they demo a stock watchlist scanner, show how to spend more compute on the phases that matter, walk through the Bug Hunter and Explainer Studio templates, and explain why single agents fail through laziness, self-preference bias and goal drift. They finish with a deep dive on running agents safely at scale: budgets, interrupts, auto mode, credential vaults and network lockdown. items.excerpt: We think "did a human read the code?" is an imprecise proxy for "what could go wrong with this change, and which check—automated or human—is the right one to catch it?" Asking that question also changed when review happens. Before, review was a gate at the end of the road: write the code, open a PR, wait for your colleague. Now, review runs continuously, more like spellcheck while you write. Most changes have been reviewed and fixed by Claude at least once before a human is asked to look. This catches most routine mistakes, and saves team attention for higher-level questions and scrutiny. — Addy Osmani, Morgan Westlee Lunt, and Qing Wang , How the Claude Code team does code review Tags: anthropic , claude , ai , claude-code , llms , addy-osmani , coding-agents , generative-ai , agentic-engineering , code-review

items.author: @levie
items.subtitle: Aaron Levie · ceo @box - your business lives in content.…
items.text: Moving from chatting back and forth with agents, to having agents that you spin up in the background to do useful work for you is probably on the order of 100X or 1000X more token consumption than what we’re seeing today. Most work right now is essentially rate limited by our ability to process and work with information. Moving data between systems. Reviewing a document. Looking through code for security issues. Processing log data to look for even patterns. Looking up information about a prospective client. Almost all of knowledge work is constrained by these steps, and AI has become a huge unlock to that. So our first step was to use AI to do these individual tasks much faster for us. That was the chatbot phenomenon that we have been experiencing for the past 3+ years. But we can still then only augment the work that we remain in the loop for, and we’re highly limited by our ability to parallelize this work by our own bandwidth and context. But where we’re going is quite different. As AI models continue to improve at incredible rates, we can hand off more and more work to the agent. First it’s letting the agent run with a harder problem. Then it’s giving a few agents multiple parts of a task at once. But we’re not far off from being able to throw an arbitrary number of agents at a problem and just say “come back when you’ve accomplished this goal”. Now imagine that agent swarm for any problem we can think of. Protecting our codebases, data, and systems. QAing every change we make and make sure all our infrastructure is robust and does what it should. Looking through every document for potential risks. Auditing this company with vastly more data reviewed. And on and on. Most of this isn’t even replacing existing work we do, it’s all net new. These agents will get deployed as swarms by people, by workflows, by triggers, and by other agents. And none of this would be possible if the models weren’t getting better, and if the cost of AI didn’t make it affordable. Both of those trends though are playing out. Now the next frontier is just having enough compute. But this is where it’s heading.

items.text: This is one of the most exhilarating times in technology, and this challenge was yet another jaw-dropping moment. When the details of OpenAI’s agent escape and Hugging Face hack started to emerge, it became clear that agent containment would be one of the most important priorities for any AI infra company. There are two classes of escapes: ① "escape the network" and ② “escape the matrix” 😁, as in, break the spell of virtualization. OpenAI was the former, where an agent not supposed to have internet access… gained it by hacking another system. Genuinely astonishing and worrisome. Through this challenge, however, we discovered something even more groundbreaking. A talented white-hat researcher, armed with a swarm of AI agents, expertise and perseverance, "pierced through" the Linux virtualization boundary that nearly every cloud sandbox provider in the world banks on today. I'm very thankful we got the report, were able to quickly move to protect our customers, found no evidence of customer data compromise, and collaborated with many industry partners to protect the wider internet. Our confidence and conviction in Vercel Sandbox are even greater now, after some of the smartest, most motivated researchers in the world, and their agents, gave it their best shot.

items.title: Anthropic tells investors quarterly revenue up nearly 50% to $16.8bn ahead of IPO
items.excerpt: Anthropic tells investors quarterly revenue up nearly 50% to $16.8bn ahead of IPO The phrase "told investors" appears four times in this FT article, which reports on Anthropic's day of hosting investors on Wednesday. Lots of details in here from " people with knowledge of the matter ". Key things I learned from the article: Q1 revenue (Jan/Feb/Mar) was "about $4.8bn" Q2 (Apr/May/Jun) was $11.5bn Q3 (Jul/Aug/Sep) was $16.8bn In Q3: $1.70 in revenue for every $1 spent on "computing power" Adjusted operating margins (excluding stock-based compensation) were 11% This point about distillation is worth quoting in full (highlight mine): The start-up has also clamped down on “distillation” — a controversial practice whereby rival AI labs train their models on the outputs of more advanced ones. When rival companies “distil” their models from Anthropic’s models, that involves heavy usage and spending. Anthropic told investors on Wednesday distillation accounted for 5 per cent to 7 per cent of revenue and that they had cut it back “materially” in the third quarter of the year, said four people with direct knowledge of the matter. Napkin maths says that if distillation was 5% of their Q2 revenue (before they cut it back in Q3) then unnamed "other labs" spent over half a billion dollars distilling Anthropic's models in that quarter! Also notable: Anthropic appear to no longer be leaning on "annualized run-rate revenue" ( previously ) in these communications to their investors. Tags: ai , generative-ai , llms , anthropic

items.title: Paving the Road to Production: Governed Enterprise AI Agents — Harish Gaggar, Credit Karma
items.excerpt: Register an agent through an internal portal and receive more than a repository: the deployment also needs identity, memory, traces, evaluations and secret handling. Harish Gaggar walks through that paved path for enterprise agents at Intuit Credit Karma. Local development progresses through container builds, review, security scanning and Kubernetes deployment, with the supporting resources provisioned consistently. The architecture places a centralized MCP gateway between agents and tools so authentication and routing are part of every request. Custom MCP servers expose reviewed tools, while OpenTelemetry, Tempo, Prometheus and Grafana make failures, latency and access behavior visible. Gaggar then follows a LangGraph workflow from interpretation and planning through evidence gathering, policy checks and human approval for sensitive actions. Threads, runs and checkpoints preserve state, while separate tracking tables record model use, tool calls, costs and evaluation fields. Demonstrations inspect those records rather than establish a validated quality score for the whole system. A PII filtering layer aims to intercept sensitive inputs before they reach models, memory or traces; detection and redaction remain controls to evaluate, rather than a guarantee that no secret can escape. The final component prunes, reranks, deduplicates and compresses context. Its examples show large token reductions, including about 90% in a demonstrated query, without a paired answer quality study or measured business ROI. The practical point is to build the surrounding framework from the start, giving each agent a consistent route through access control, observability, durable state and accountable action. items.title: How to Actually Tokenmaxx and Save Millions — Alvin Pane, OutRival
items.excerpt: A cheaper candidate model disagrees with the production model on 18% of examples. Reject it immediately, or first ask how often production disagrees with itself? Alvin Pane uses that question to frame a token optimization workflow at OutRival. Repeated runs of the existing model reveal a reported 7% disagreement rate, making simple model to model agreement an incomplete quality measure. His HarborBite example is a synthetic proxy for a large instruction prompt, used to show the mechanics of reducing cost while preserving the application's required behavior. It is not evidence of realized million dollar savings. Pane starts with observability: record prompt versions, model choices, tokens, latency and costs before changing them. Prefix caching removes avoidable repeated work. DSPy and GEPA can then search for shorter instructions, preserving the interface and scoring contract rather than simply deleting text. The illustrated prompt shrinks by 51%, but that reduction still needs a quality test. A smaller model may fit a narrow benchmark and fail on unfamiliar inputs. Shadow evaluation therefore compares production with itself, the candidate with itself and both systems on the same requests. Human review of disagreements separates regressions from improvements and ambiguous cases. A paired confidence interval around the net gain supplies a release criterion, with critical customer categories checked separately so an overall average cannot hide damage to an important task. The closing rule is to keep measuring after release: cheaper instructions and tokens matter only when the system continues to perform the work users need. items.title: I Spent Two Years Building the Median — Hariprasad Sudharshan
items.excerpt: After two years of intense solo building, Hariprasad Sudharshan discovers that other people have independently produced calculators much like his own. Nobody needs to have copied anyone: the same models, tools and familiar problem can lead builders toward the same solution. He calls that shared starting point the median. Faster development makes it easier to ship useful software, including internal tools and learning projects, but a functioning demo does not establish a durable product advantage. His talk is a personal reflection on that distinction, rather than a controlled study of product success or a disclosed business outcome. Sudharshan separates the model's capability from its harness and the product a customer ultimately receives. He describes a build first reflex that replaces searching for existing solutions with immediately opening a coding agent. His alternative is a novelty budget: name the one distinctive thing before starting, include it in the roadmap and review it as deliberately as other project spending. For leaders evaluating demos, he proposes three questions. Who has already solved this? What does this team have that a competitor does not? Where will the application reach users? A later calculator iteration focuses on the difference between running open model weights inside an enterprise and purchasing inference, including utilization and the infrastructure between weights and generated tokens. The practical lesson is to use the readily available starting point where it helps, then spend judgment on a specific problem, distribution and a defensible difference. items.subtitle: Aaron Levie · ceo @box - your business lives in content.…
items.text: At Box, we've been testing Gemini 4 Argon on our Box AI Complex Work eval for the past week. It's a huge upgrade over Gemini 3.1 Pro, jumping by 14 percentage points across all our tests, and firmly at the frontier. In our evaluation, we give the Box Agent (using Gemini 4 Argon) a variety of complex enterprise tasks involving enterprise documents in a range of industries. These tasks approximate the kind of hard, time-consuming work that knowledge workers do every day with their enterprise content. Gemini 4 is a huge leap on effectively every dimension of this work. Gemini 4 is far more capable on math, logic, analytics, and deep knowledge of a variety of business domains. It also works far harder to complete tasks fully without stopping short of the desired result. This is incredibly important for complex enterprise workflows that depend on robust task execution. Here are some example wins that we saw to put the improvements in perspective: * Financial services (+18 points): a funding-gap analysis for a family-owned company, where the brief spelled out every step of the projected statements, down to the interest on the bank loan and the overdraft for each year. Gemini 4 Argon built them exactly as specified, every line broken out and carried through to the funding gap. Gemini 3.1 Pro folded the interest into a single figure. * Healthcare (+25 points): an intensive care management plan where both models spotted a dangerous potassium level and a drug interaction. Only Gemini 4 Argon went back and pulled the offending drugs from the final regimen, so its plan actually matched its own diagnosis. * Technology (+37 points): a product performance review deciding which of two regional markets should have its cloud infrastructure optimized first. Gemini 4 Argon pulled the right month's user, retention and per-user figures for both regions and correctly flagged North America. Gemini 3.1 Pro often pulled the wrong rows, at one point reporting retention above 100%, and pointed the effort at the wrong region. * Energy (+16 points): an energy consumption report across two facilities that had to flag any gaps in the meter data. Gemini 4 Argon consistently caught that the data center's smart meter log stops in November. Gemini 3.1 Pro often missed it, at times declaring the logs complete. * Consumer products (+33 points): a product launch evaluation deciding which production expansion to fund. Gemini 4 Argon saw that existing inventory could bridge an early capacity gap, which made the smaller expansion viable with an earlier launch and a faster break-even. Gemini 3.1 Pro defaulted to the larger expansion and the later timeline. Gemini 4 Argon will be available in the Box AI Studio shortly for anyone to build custom Box Agents with.

items.title: AI is mass decompiling games. That's both awesome and scary.
items.excerpt: AI is mass decompiling games. That's both awesome and scary. Indie game developer Popcar talks about the recent wave of AI-powered decompilation of existing games, enabling weird mashups between existing games, and producing a boom in game preservation projects to get old games working on new hardware (often in a browser using WebAssembly). I like how this piece captures both the positives and the negatives of this new development: Most people already realized the scary part by now. If AI can decompile games and software, then the entire tech industry is about to explode. Anybody can decompile other software and use it any way they'd like, and nobody can stop them. Companies can steal from competitors. Your paid game or app can be open-sourced against your will. This isn't exclusive to old video games, we can apply this to any software. [...] This is also a big win for preservation. Old games can be ported, modified, enhanced, and made much more easily accessible than before. [...[ With console makers going all in on digital and games becoming entirely unplayable due to servers shutting down, this is fantastic news. We could own software we bought regardless of what the company thinks. Via Hacker News Tags: computer-history , game-design , ai , webassembly , generative-ai , llms , ai-ethics , coding-agents

items.title: I Believe Everything My Agents Tell Me: Three Levels of Review — Corey Gallon, Rexmore
items.excerpt: A demand letter passed its drafting agent's own checks, yet two independent reviewer agents found that the supposedly expired contract had renewed less than three weeks earlier. Sending it could have left the business owing thousands of dollars. Corey Gallon uses that case to explain a three level review method for agents that overstate completed work, misread facts or draw the wrong conclusions. His analysis of his own 2026 sessions found a consequential error in about four out of ten sessions; that is a description of his sample, not an error rate for all agents or for the final reviewed outputs. Level one requires a verified artifact with a fingerprint, or an explicit account of what is missing. Level two has independent agents extract the same material against a control total, then settles every difference against the source. For a year of scanned accounting statements, that process found 56 differences and produced records that balanced to the penny. Level three combines a self audit, cold reviewer agents with reasons to challenge the work and fresh reviewers for the revision. A memory leak investigation exposed a flawed reproduction and an overstated fix before the maintainer merged the corrected change. Gallon reports the time and token costs for these cases and releases the method as agent skills. The evidence supports a concrete checking workflow, rather than a guarantee that review eliminates every error. items.title: The Agent Works. Does Anyone Trust It? — Michele Grant, Leading at Scale
items.excerpt: An agent's reports match the analysts' work during a pilot, yet the steering committee still has to decide whether it should operate in a core business process. Michele Grant uses an illustrative acquisition integration scenario to examine that decision. The question moves beyond technical accuracy to measurable value, accountable ownership and evidence for greater authority. A faster report is useful only if it changes a decision or releases capacity that the organization actually redeploys. Her framework starts with a baseline for reporting time, analyst capacity, operating cost and the detection of material issues, so an attractive demo does not become its own business case. Grant separates the people who operate the workflow, oversee its risk and provide independent assurance. A Human Works Standard records what the agent may do, where human judgment remains necessary and who must intervene when something goes wrong. An auditable decision log, a maintained inventory of agents and dependencies, and an autonomy scorecard make those boundaries reviewable. Financial calculations stay in deterministic code while the model helps with narrative and interpretation. Authority advances through shadow operation, reviewed drafts, exception handling with sampling and finally exception focused review supported by independent checks. At that last stage, missed issues matter as much as flagged ones. A falling override rate can reflect weaker review rather than better performance. The acquisition values and capacity examples explain the operating framework; they are not disclosed results from a completed deployment or proof that the agent created the projected synergies. items.title: Deploying AI Inside a Bank Is Not an Engineering Problem — Paden Gayle, Applied AI Engineers
items.excerpt: A bank's document exception assistant produces a convincing demo, but security, data owners and risk reviewers still cannot approve it. Paden Gayle uses that hypothetical project to show why a working model does not establish a route into production. The missing decisions concern where the system runs, who authorized the documents, who reviews a wrong exception and which existing controls the workflow must satisfy. Drawing on his engineering experience, Gayle makes discovery part of the build: find the people who own those decisions in the first week, then define the smallest useful system they can evaluate. When a customer cannot supply a complete specification, his method is to shadow the work, draft a concrete workflow and shrink it with the control owners. Autonomy starts with the least authority needed to solve the problem. A drafting assistant can gather evidence about errors, overrides and recovery before anyone grants it permission to take further actions. Gayle also outlines an evidence pack covering intended use, data lineage, failure modes, results by segment and accountable controls. Original inputs and outputs belong in that record; rerunning a model later cannot reconstruct exactly what happened. Aggregate performance can conceal a poorly supported document type or user group, so weak segments need explicit restrictions. The closing checklist turns unresolved approval decisions into named owners and next steps. It is a planning aid for deployment, rather than a claim that the illustrative bank project shipped or that a checklist guarantees approval. items.text: Agent swarms are going to be a core part of many enterprise workflows in the future. The ability to throw compute at problems that you can massively parallelize will be too useful to not take advantage of. Cyber will be one of the biggest beneficiaries of this as it’s a space where testing vast number of permutations of attacks (without getting tired or bored) is an incredibly useful property. You have a wide search space of possible risk vectors and you generally need to be able to chain together different scenarios to achieve the exploit. This will become one of the biggest token uses in large enterprises given the range of IT systems, software, physical infrastructure, and data that needs to be protected at all times. Super interesting times in cyber.

items.title: Agents in Orbit: Workflows, Not Autopilot — Eduardo Simon & Javier Casal, Flywire
items.excerpt: More than 9,700 code review runs in 30 days came from a workflow that lets the model read code but never modify it. Eduardo Simon and Javier Casal describe Orbit, Flywire's internal platform for putting model steps inside deterministic engineering workflows. A YAML definition goes through the same merge request review as other code, declares the tools and access each step can use, and runs on the company's existing deployment infrastructure. The predictable work stays in code; a model supplies the judgment. Human review of merge requests remains part of the process as the platform expands across roughly 400 engineers. Code review, translation updates, dependency fixes, ticket triage and bulk repository changes show the range of tasks this pattern supports. The architecture separates orchestration, execution and session state, then adds timeouts, rate limits and locks against duplicate runs. Per step restrictions cover network access, tools, skills and MCP servers, while structured outputs drive subsequent branches. The speakers are candid about the remaining work: new workflows initially receive a few real case checks, golden datasets run on demand, online evaluations are still being built and full sandboxing is a goal. Their reported execution success rate does not establish answer correctness. The practical adoption path starts with a useful skill, proves the recurring task and then turns it into a background workflow with explicit ownership and review. items.excerpt: Agents are starting to pick your vendors, and most signup flows block them at the door. NEXT UP: AI ENGINEER CODE SUMMIT Join us in SF for the second annual AIE CODE Summit, Nov 10–12, our last flagship summit of 2026. Applications live now: https://aie.codes Michael Grinich, founder and CEO of WorkOS, argues that as agents run for hours and increasingly choose tools on their own, services have to make something agents want. items.text: This is a good way to understand how early we actually are in AI diffusion right now. The vast majority of people are using AI as a chatbot for simple interactions that approximate next-generation search. This is super useful but dramatically underrepresents the full capability of AI. On the complete other end of the spectrum, agent swarms represent possibly the ultimate form factor of what agents will do inside of our workflows. Math, cyber, bio, materials science, software engineering, finance, and any other field that has valuable tasks that can be executed in parallel where compute can be applied to accelerate work all have this characteristic. Less than a fraction of a fraction of the population uses AI in this way right now, due to a mix of the capabilities of models relative to the user's domain, the cost of doing these types of workflows today, the harnesses available to do this style of AI work, and the availability (or lack thereof) of frontier models to the general public. There will also be a huge amount of change management necessary to get most areas of work -beyond software and AI research- to benefit from this style of agents. Companies need to upgrade their workflows, data needs to integrated and migrated into modern platforms, and companies will need to work through compliance, governance, and security frameworks to pull it off. But this all represents opportunity right now. A lot of this is where the applied layer of AI will really shine in the enterprise because of the domain specificity of this type of work. You can get an early sense of where things are going and the opportunity ahead by seeing through the funnel that Andrej lays out.

items.text: "I'm not at a point where I trust the agent, especially with stuff that people are using." From Micky (@Rasmic), who's taught 100K+ people to build with AI: "The manual review is like the final step. All the work's done, and I have as much evidence from the agent as possible. With evidence-driven testing, before and after, and even greploop, we're trying to build trust. The agent presents evidence: This is the work that's done, and this is why it's good. For anyone who's been a developer for any time, manual review is probably the worst part of your job. This sort of helps minimize the friction." 📌 Watch Micky's full 4-step workflow here: https://t.co/ju9aMQKaCE

items.author: @karpathy
items.subtitle: Andrej Karpathy
items.text: Dusting off this tweet from April because this gap in shared understanding of LLM capability is *widening*. It's now less "two groups of people speaking past each other" and more a sharp funnel. - Napkin math somewhere around 6B people (~75% of the population) have barely come in contact with LLMs at all. - Around 1-2B (~20%) are casual and infrequent users of free-tier ChatGPT-like products. This group sees derpy chatbots and treats them a bit like a better Google search, a writing aid, or etc. Maybe an agent tries to book you a flight. I have non-tech friends who (reasonably, imo) say they have not much use for it at all. Even many professionals outside of math&code are in this tier. For example, execs and many other functions spend a lot of their time talking to other people, so while they understand what is happening intellectually, it is still second-hand and a bit abstract. - Now we get to professional use of frontier-grade LLMs in math&code. Somewhere around 20M people (0.2%) see first-hand that large, complex projects that used to take them weeks/months can now be completed by agents with a prompt. Building apps, copying apps, translating apps, decompiling apps from binaries... This has all happened very quickly and recently - less than 1 year ago, I was writing code manually by hand, typing memorized computer code commands into a code editor character by character, occasionally pressing Tab to autocomplete a little chunk of code. - And finally we get to the ~5,000 people (~0.00006%) with access to frontier-grade systems internally. The external world has seen the preview. It looks like swarms of thousands of agents collaborating over weeks on software mega projects: minting zero days, running cyber attacks and defenses at machine speeds, discovering new science, advancing the frontier of mathematics. Things that would have taken top professionals in the industry years of work. Meanwhile, human review and comprehension are starting to fall behind. For example, people are still involved in the "archeology" of the OpenAI-HF incident from many months ago. Mathematicians may be poring over the 722 manuscripts on frontier mathematics for a while. The funnel is driven by a combination of factors: 1. The impact scales with ambition, problem size, and horizon. A question with a paragraph answer barely stresses the system. You need a reservoir of big, difficult problems that you really care about. This aspect drives the consumer / professional dimension of the funnel. 2. The jaggedness of the system (which I have written about a lot separately). Capability peaks in domains that are digital, verifiable and economically valuable. This is because LLM capability emerges from reinforcement learning on verifiable rewards on a curated environment mixture driven by revenue potential. This aspect primarily drives the area (e.g. math&code) dimension of the funnel. 3. Access. Free-tier, paid-tier, internal. So this is the weirdness of the moment. The general public has mostly not interacted with these systems. When they have, it looks like a derpy chatbot. The majority of professionals still see only a modest uplift. And a small sliver of professionals are experiencing the vertigo of the curve going vertical. And it is all happening at the same time.
